javelina.diet: Pencas de nopal, vainas de mezquite, corazones de agave, raíces y tubérculos
javelina.shelter: La manada se echa a la sombra de un matorral espinoso denso o bajo un saliente rocoso durante las horas de calor
javelina.preferredHabitat: Matorral desértico y arroyos secos con cobertura espinosa densa y macizos de nopal
javelina.fact: Un pecarí se come el nopal entero —espinas incluidas— y tiene en el lomo una glándula de olor tan fuerte que la manada puede encontrarse en la oscuridad solo por el olfato.
javelina.role: Los pecaríes son los procesadores de cactus del desierto: trituran pencas que ninguna otra cosa toca, lo que impide que el nopal se apodere de un arroyo seco, y esparcen sus semillas en el excremento. Al hozar en busca de tubérculos voltean el suelo endurecido y entierran hojarasca, dándoles a las semillas dónde germinar después de la lluvia. Andan en manadas de seis a doce, y el olor de la manada es también su sistema de alarma, porque ven pésimo.
javelina.hint: Haz crecer el nopal y deja una maraña espinosa con sombra donde echarse. La manada duerme el mediodía y sale a comer al atardecer.

black-swift.name: Vencejo negro
black-swift.diet: Hormigas voladoras, pulgones, escarabajos y efímeras capturados en pleno vuelo, a menudo a cientos de metros de altura
black-swift.shelter: Una copa de musgo pegada a una grieta mojada de la roca detrás o junto a una caída de agua, a la que solo se llega por el aire
black-swift.preferredHabitat: Acantilados con agua fría corriendo por ellos y cielo abierto por encima del límite arbóreo
black-swift.fact: Un vencejo negro puede pasar seis meses en el aire sin posarse ni una vez: come, bebe y duerme volando, y el pollito se queda solo todo el día mientras sus padres cazan insectos a 50 km de distancia.
black-swift.role: Los vencejos aspiran los enjambres de insectos que el aire ascendente sube a la montaña, y llevan esa comida de vuelta convertida en una bolita comprimida: una entrega al día le basta al pollito porque la carga viene concentradísima. El nido tiene que estar permanentemente mojado y ser inalcanzable, así que solo aparecen donde hay una grieta de acantilado con agua corriéndole encima. Están entre los últimos visitantes del verano en llegar y los primeros en irse hacia el Amazonas.
black-swift.hint: Busca la grieta más mojada y oscura del acantilado y mantén el agua corriendo por ella. Aquí no anida nada que pueda llegar caminando.

peregrine-falcon.name: Halcón peregrino
peregrine-falcon.diet: Otras aves capturadas en pleno vuelo: lagópodos, pinzones montañeses, vencejos, bisbitas y patos pequeños
peregrine-falcon.shelter: Un simple hoyo raspado con las patas en la grava de una cornisa alta; no construye nido alguno
peregrine-falcon.preferredHabitat: Acantilados y paredes de roca a plomo sobre terreno abierto con muchas aves volando abajo
peregrine-falcon.fact: Un halcón peregrino en picada alcanza unos 380 km/h, lo que lo convierte en el animal más veloz del planeta, y tiene unos conos de hueso en las fosas nasales que frenan el aire para que la picada no le reviente los pulmones.
peregrine-falcon.role: El halcón peregrino es el cazador aéreo de la montaña y captura casi toda su comida en el aire, golpeando desde arriba con el puño cerrado en vez de agarrar. Como caza aves y nada más, es un freno directo a las bandadas de pinzones, bisbitas y lagópodos que se alimentan por las laderas. Necesita una cornisa de acantilado sin perturbar y aire despejado por debajo, y nada con qué construir: solo grava suelta donde raspar un hoyo.
peregrine-falcon.hint: Una cornisa alta con grava suelta encima y cielo abierto por debajo. No construyas un nido: aquí basta con patear un hoyito en la gravilla.

owl-limpet.name: Galleta de mar
owl-limpet.diet: Algas, plancton y restos de comida recogidos de la arena, grano a grano
owl-limpet.shelter: Medio enterrada de canto en la arena ondulada, en lechos de cientos a la vez
owl-limpet.preferredHabitat: Fondos de arena resguardados justo por debajo de la línea de bajamar, donde la corriente es suave
owl-limpet.fact: Una galleta de mar viva no es blanca ni lisa: es morada y está cubierta de diminutas espinas que se mueven, con las que camina y se pasa la comida hasta la boca. El disco blanco con dibujo de flor es su esqueleto, después de que todo lo demás se lavó.
owl-limpet.role: Un lecho entero se para medio enterrado de canto, como monedas en una ranura, todas inclinadas hacia la corriente para atrapar lo que pasa a la deriva. Donde el agua es más brava se acuestan de plano, para que no las hagan rodar.
owl-limpet.hint: Arena limpia y ondulada justo por debajo de la línea de marea, en un sitio lo bastante resguardado como para que la corriente sea suave.

octopus.name: Pulpo
octopus.diet: Cangrejos de orilla, almejas, mejillones, caracoles y camarones, abiertos a la fuerza o perforados
octopus.shelter: Una grieta o una concha vacía a la que le arrastra una roca por detrás, con un montón de conchas vacías afuera de la puerta
octopus.preferredHabitat: Fondo rocoso submareal y pozas de marea profundas con muchas grietas y agua fría y limpia
octopus.fact: Un pulpo tiene tres corazones, sangre azul y saborea con los brazos todo lo que toca; y como lo único duro que tiene es el pico, uno del tamaño de un plato puede colarse por un agujero del tamaño de una uva.
octopus.role: El pulpo es el máximo cazador invertebrado de la costa rocosa, y el montón de conchas vacías de cangrejo y almeja frente a su guarida es la forma más fácil de encontrar uno. Puede cambiar de color y de textura de piel en menos de un segundo para desaparecer contra la roca o el kelp, aunque no distingue los colores; y a una almeja terca le perfora un agujero limpio y le inyecta algo para que la concha se relaje. Cada pulpo despacha una cantidad enorme de cangrejos, lo que mantiene a raya a los herbívoros y carroñeros de las pozas de marea.
octopus.hint: Roca partida con huecos donde esconderse, y muchos cangrejos. Deja en paz el montón de conchas de la entrada: así es como sabes que hay alguien en casa.

grasshopper-mouse.name: Ratón saltamontes
grasshopper-mouse.diet: Escorpiones, ciempiés, escarabajos y otros ratones
grasshopper-mouse.shelter: Se apodera de una madriguera que excavó otro animal y luego la defiende
grasshopper-mouse.preferredHabitat: Planicies arenosas abiertas con matorral disperso y presas de sobra bajo las patas
grasshopper-mouse.fact: Este ratón caza escorpiones, recibe picaduras en la cara y sigue comiendo: su cuerpo apaga la señal de dolor del veneno. Después se para en las patas traseras y le aúlla a la luna como un lobito.
grasshopper-mouse.role: Un ratón que decidió ser depredador. Mantiene a raya a los escorpiones y a los insectos grandes, y es uno de los pocos animales capaces de comerse a los habitantes más venenosos del desierto sin inmutarse.
grasshopper-mouse.hint: Una madriguera vieja de la cual apoderarse y terreno abierto donde cazar. Toda el agua que necesita la saca de lo que atrapa.

snow-bunting.name: Escribano nival
snow-bunting.diet: Semillas arrastradas por el viento sobre la nieve, además de insectos durante el corto verano
snow-bunting.shelter: En lo hondo de una grieta de roca, forrada con plumas y pelo contra el frío
snow-bunting.preferredHabitat: Crestas barridas por el viento y pedregal donde la nieve no se acumula
snow-bunting.fact: Los escribanos nivales anidan más al norte que cualquier otra ave canora de la Tierra, tan metidos en las grietas de la roca que el macho tiene que alimentar a la hembra a oscuras mientras ella empolla.
snow-bunting.role: Un ave pequeña que trata una ventisca como si fuera clima normal. Las bandadas recorren las crestas peladas recogiendo la semilla que el viento dejó varada sobre la nieve, y pasan del blanco al marrón cálido conforme cambia la estación.
snow-bunting.hint: Una grieta honda y seca en la roca, a resguardo del viento, y terreno pedregoso abierto cerca donde la nieve no cuaje.

groundhog.name: Marmota
groundhog.diet: Pasto, trébol, dientes de león y casi cualquier cosa verde y tierna a su alcance
groundhog.shelter: Una madriguera con varias entradas, una cámara para dormir forrada de pasto y un cuarto aparte que usa de baño
groundhog.preferredHabitat: Bordes de pradera con suelo profundo y bien drenado por donde pueda excavar
groundhog.fact: Una marmota excava una madriguera con puerta de entrada, puerta de atrás, dormitorio y un cuarto aparte para ir al baño, y mueve cerca de una tonelada de tierra al hacerlo. En invierno su corazón baja a unos cinco latidos por minuto.
groundhog.role: La excavadora de la pradera. Sus madrigueras abandonadas se vuelven casas para zorros, serpientes, conejos y la mitad de los animales pequeños de aquí, así que lo que excava una sola sigue sirviendo años después de que se fue.
groundhog.hint: Suelo profundo y bien drenado al borde del pasto, con un refugio de escape cerca. Aquí importa más dónde excavar que dónde esconderse.

opossum.name: Zarigüeya
opossum.diet: Casi cualquier cosa: insectos, fruta, huevos, carroña y una cantidad enorme de garrapatas
opossum.shelter: Pasa el día durmiendo en un tronco hueco o una madriguera prestada, y casi nunca usa la misma dos veces
opossum.preferredHabitat: Bordes con matorral, madera hueca, agua cerca y mucho que carroñear
opossum.fact: Cuando una zarigüeya se hace la muerta no está actuando: se desmaya. El cuerpo se le pone rígido, le cuelga la lengua y despide un olor a cosa muerta hace rato, y no puede salir de ese estado durante varios minutos, aunque te alejes.
opossum.role: El equipo de limpieza de la pradera. Come lo que todos los demás dejaron, incluida la carroña y cantidades enormes de garrapatas, y es el único animal de aquí que carga a sus crías en el lomo.
opossum.hint: Madera hueca donde dormir el día y bayas a una noche de camino. Cambia de casa todo el tiempo, así que dale más de una opción.

alpine-springtail.diet: Dead leaves and stems, fungus threads, pollen, and the pink algae that grows on old snow
alpine-springtail.shelter: Wet dead leaves, moss, and the gap between the snow and the ground in winter
alpine-springtail.preferredHabitat: Damp mountain grass, moss, and wet leaves. Also the top of old snow on warm days
alpine-springtail.fact: On a mild winter day, snow fleas pour onto the snow in their thousands. It looks like spilled pepper. Their blood is full of antifreeze, so they keep moving when everything else is frozen stiff.
alpine-springtail.role: The clean-up crew. Without them, last year's leaves would pile up forever. They chew dead stems and graze fungus threads into soil. They keep at it all winter, in the dark gap under the snow. Pipits, finches, chickadees, bluebirds, nutcrackers, and toads all eat them.
alpine-springtail.hint: A mat of dead leaves under melting snow. That is enough to start.

purple-sea-urchin.diet: Living kelp and surfgrass, loose kelp that drifts by, and hard pink algae on the rock
purple-sea-urchin.shelter: A pit it grinds into the rock with its own teeth and spines
purple-sea-urchin.preferredHabitat: Rock near kelp, low down the shore, with waves washing over it
purple-sea-urchin.fact: A purple urchin chews a pit into solid rock with five teeth. Then it sits in that pit for years. On some reefs, urchins wear away more stone than the waves do.
purple-sea-urchin.role: This grazer sits at the heart of the coast's most famous story. Otters keep their numbers down, and scraps of loose kelp keep them fed. Then they are just one more part of a healthy forest. Take the hunters away and they march up the rock. They mow the kelp down to bare stone and leave an empty desert behind.
purple-sea-urchin.hint: Kelp first. There has to be something to eat. Then think hard about what will keep the grazers in check.

northern-anchovy.diet: Plankton: tiny animals, plant cells, and larvae, strained from the water or picked off one at a time
northern-anchovy.shelter: The school itself. Open water near shore, with kelp and surfgrass edges as cover for the young
northern-anchovy.preferredHabitat: Cool water near shore with plenty of plankton in it
northern-anchovy.fact: An anchovy eats in two ways. It can snap at big prey one bite at a time. Or it can open its mouth and swim, straining the sea like a living net.
northern-anchovy.role: Anchovies swim in silver schools so thick they turn the water dark from below. Almost every hunter here takes them at some point: pelicans, seals, dolphins, gulls. So when the anchovies fail, the whole coast goes hungry at once.
northern-anchovy.hint: Cold water rising from the deep grows the plankton they eat. Quiet shallows give the schools a place to lay eggs.

beach-hopper.diet: Rotting kelp and other seaweed washed up at the tide line
beach-hopper.shelter: Burrows dug in damp sand high up the beach, and the wet underside of kelp and driftwood
beach-hopper.preferredHabitat: A gently sloping sandy beach with the seaweed left where it lands
beach-hopper.fact: Beach hoppers spend all day shut inside a burrow in dry sand. After dark they pour out to shred the seaweed the tide left behind. Step near one and it fires into the air like a flicked pebble.
beach-hopper.role: The engine room of the beach. Hoppers chew washed-up kelp down into crumbs. That turns dead seaweed into bird food, which is the whole reason plovers, sanderlings, and gulls walk the tide line. Rake the seaweed away and this link is gone overnight.
beach-hopper.hint: Leave the seaweed where the tide drops it. That is the whole meal.

desert-termite.diet: Dead grass, fallen leaves, dry dung, and the weathered outside of dead wood
desert-termite.shelter: Tunnels and rooms underground, plus a mud roof built over whatever it is eating
desert-termite.preferredHabitat: Soil under shrubs and grass where dead leaves and stems pile up
desert-termite.fact: These termites spread a thin mud roof over a dead stem and eat under it. That way they can feed in full sun and never touch the dry air.
desert-termite.role: This is the animal that recycles the desert. There is too little water here for dead plants to rot the way they do in a forest. So termites eat almost all of it instead. They carry the goodness back underground. They also leave tunnels that let rain soak in instead of running off. On the nights they swarm, everything with a beak or a sting comes to feed.
desert-termite.hint: Bury a little dead wood and they will find it. Dead wood is the desert's pantry.

common-raven.diet: Dead animals most of all, plus eggs, chicks, young reptiles, bugs, and cactus fruit
common-raven.shelter: A big stick nest on a cliff, in a tall cactus, or in a thorny tree. More and more often, on power poles
common-raven.preferredHabitat: Open desert with tall places to nest and food it can count on
common-raven.fact: Ravens remember single human faces and hold the grudge for years. A pair will even run a trick together. One bird makes a fuss while the other steals the food.
common-raven.role: The clean-up crew, and the biggest human story in the desert. Roads, dumps, farms, and power poles hand ravens free food, water, and places to nest. So there are far more of them than this desert could ever feed on its own. All those extra ravens eat baby tortoises, whose shells stay soft for years. Cutting off the free meals is now a real part of saving the tortoise.
common-raven.hint: They follow whatever gets left lying around: a dead animal, a tall perch, something to drink. That is all they ask for, and that is the trouble.

coyote-meadow.diet: Voles, rabbits, and ground squirrels; young deer; also fruit, bugs, and dead animals
coyote-meadow.shelter: Raises pups in a den dug into a brushy bank, often an old badger or fox hole made bigger
coyote-meadow.preferredHabitat: Open grassland and edges with brushy cover for a den, and water close by
coyote-meadow.fact: Three coyotes can sound like a dozen. Each one slides its voice up and down as it howls. So a small family throws up a wall of sound. Scientists call it the 'beau geste' trick.
coyote-meadow.role: The top hunter of this meadow, and the one that copes with anything. It hunts voles and rabbits alone. It hunts young deer in pairs. In between it eats fruit, bugs, and dead animals. Its return finally puts pressure on the foxes, badgers, and deer that nothing else here could touch. It will even trail a digging badger and grab whatever bolts out the far side.
coyote-meadow.hint: A brushy bank for a den, wide grass full of rabbits and voles, and water close by. This is the last piece. It only moves in where there is already plenty to eat.

polyphemus-moth.diet: Tree leaves when it is a caterpillar: oak, birch, hickory, maple, and willow. The grown moth has no working mouth and never eats at all
polyphemus-moth.shelter: Spins a tough silk cocoon wrapped in a leaf. The cocoon falls with the leaves in autumn and lies on the forest floor all winter
polyphemus-moth.preferredHabitat: Broadleaf woods and woodland edges with oak, birch, and hickory, and deep leaves left lying below
polyphemus-moth.fact: The grown moth has no mouth. It cannot eat one single thing. Everything it will ever spend on finding a mate and laying eggs was eaten months before, by the caterpillar.
polyphemus-moth.role: This moth stands for the caterpillar layer. Nearly every forest bird depends on that step. Caterpillars turn tough, chewy tree leaves into soft protein. And it is caterpillars, not seeds, that woodland songbirds stuff into their chicks. The adults that make it feed bats at dusk. The cocoons spend all winter down in the fallen leaves. So a wood raked bare in autumn throws next summer's moths out with the leaf bags.
polyphemus-moth.hint: Broadleaf trees for the caterpillars to eat, and leaves left lying all winter for the cocoons hidden among them.

amphipod.diet: Dead leaves and stems, the fungus and germs growing on them, and algae scraped off water plants
amphipod.shelter: Among sunken dead leaves, plant stems, and the loose mud on top
amphipod.preferredHabitat: Shallow water with plenty of air in it and a deep drift of rotting leaves
amphipod.fact: Freshwater shrimp swim on their sides. Males carry females around piggyback for days before they mate. Lift a handful of soggy leaves out of a pond and dozens will be flicking about in it.
amphipod.role: The marsh's shredder. One shrimp chews a single dead cattail leaf into thousands of crumbs. It is really after the fungus furring the leaf, not the leaf itself. That is how a heap of dead plants becomes food for minnows, young salamanders, and young dragonflies.
amphipod.hint: A drift of rotting leaves in still water is all they need.

crayfish.diet: Rotting plants and dead animals, live water plants, snails, insect young, and freshwater shrimp
crayfish.shelter: Burrows dug into soggy banks, and gaps under sunken logs and stones
crayfish.preferredHabitat: Slow, weedy water with sunken wood, and a bank soft enough to dig into
crayfish.fact: Lose a claw in a fight and a crayfish just grows a new one. It comes back bigger at every moult, until it matches the old one. Startle it and it flips its tail and shoots backwards, faster than you can grab.
crayfish.role: The marsh's recycler, and nearly everybody's dinner. Crayfish shred dead plants and clean up dead animals. That turns buried gunk back into living meat. Then the otter, the mink, the kingfisher, the merganser, the crane, the snapping turtle, and the heron come and take it.
crayfish.hint: A soft bank to tunnel into, sunken wood to hide under, and plenty of rotting plants to eat.

freshwater-mussel.diet: Algae, germs, and fine dead bits strained out of the water
freshwater-mussel.shelter: Buried upright in firm, fine mud with only its two tubes showing
freshwater-mussel.preferredHabitat: Slow, settled water over firm silt and fine sand
freshwater-mussel.fact: A baby mussel has to hitch a ride. It clamps onto the gills of a passing fish and rides there for weeks. Then it drops off and starts life on the bottom. Some mother mussels even wave a flap of flesh shaped like a little fish to pull a host in close.
freshwater-mussel.role: The marsh's water filter, and one of the longest-lived animals in it. One mussel can strain the same patch of water for thirty years. What it catches drops to the bottom for shrimp and crayfish. No fish means no baby mussels. So they only come back after the minnows do.
freshwater-mussel.hint: A settled bed that stays put for years. And fish, because the young ride to their new home clamped to fish gills.

pillbug.diet: Dead leaves, rotting wood, dead grass, and fungus threads. Also droppings and old bones, for the minerals
pillbug.shelter: Hides by day under crumbling logs, flat stones, and deep leaves, where the air stays damp
pillbug.preferredHabitat: Shady, damp corners of the meadow with rotting wood and a thick layer of dead leaves
pillbug.fact: A pillbug is not an insect at all. It is a crustacean, closer kin to a crab than to a beetle. It still breathes through flaps like gills, and they have to stay wet.
pillbug.role: Pillbugs work the night shift under logs and dead grass. They shred dead leaves and soft rotten wood into crumbs. Fungus and germs can then finish the job. That is the first step in turning last year's meadow into next year's soil. Garter snakes and killdeer hunt them, so the clean-up crew feeds upward as well as downward.
pillbug.hint: Damp, dark, and rotting is the whole recipe. A crumbling log, deep dead grass, and ground that never dries right out. Roll one over and it curls into a ball.

garden-spider.diet: Flying and jumping bugs caught in the web: grasshoppers, bees, flies, and moths
garden-spider.shelter: Hangs head-down in the middle of its own round web, strung between tall stems
garden-spider.preferredHabitat: Sunny meadow with tall stiff plants left standing and plenty of flying bugs
garden-spider.fact: This spider takes most of its web down every night and eats the old silk to build the next one. It also stitches a bold white zigzag through the middle, and nobody has fully worked out why.
garden-spider.role: The meadow's trapper. It slings a wheel of silk wider than your hand between tall stems. Then it waits head-down in the middle for grasshoppers, bees, and flies to blunder in. Spiders are the biggest group of hunters in any grassland. They were also the biggest thing missing from this meadow until now. They eat huge numbers of bugs, and they are the main food of half the songbirds here.
garden-spider.hint: Tall stiff stems left standing, far enough apart to sling a big web between them, with flowers close by to bring the bugs in.

big-brown-bat.diet: Bugs that fly at night, mostly beetles, plus moths, flying ants, and midges
big-brown-bat.shelter: Sleeps by day in warm dark spaces: barn lofts, attics, and under loose bark. Winters in cold cracks
big-brown-bat.preferredHabitat: Open air over meadow and hedges to hunt in, still water to drink from, and a warm sleeping spot nearby
big-brown-bat.fact: A big brown bat finds a moth in total darkness by shouting and listening to the echo. It can pick out something no thicker than a pencil lead this way.
big-brown-bat.role: The night shift over the meadow. These bats work the air above the grass and along the hedges after sunset. They catch beetles, moths, and flying ants. One bat can eat thousands of bugs in a single night. They drink on the wing, dipping their jaws into still water without stopping. Mothers gather in warm roosts to raise pups together. Great horned owls catch them at dusk.
big-brown-bat.hint: A warm crack to raise pups in, bugs in the air above the grass, and calm open water to skim a drink from without landing.

garden-snail.diet: Dead leaves, soft rotting stems, and the algae film on damp stones
garden-snail.shelter: Seals itself to the underside of a damp log or stone and waits out dry weather
garden-snail.preferredHabitat: Shady, damp corners with dead leaves and something chalky to scrape at
garden-snail.fact: A snail carries its own house and can shut the door behind it. When things get dry it glues itself to a stone and sleeps until it rains. Sometimes that takes months.
garden-snail.role: Snails are the meadow's slow recyclers. They shred fallen leaves into crumbs that fungus and soil life can finish off. When they die, their shells give calcium back to the ground.
garden-snail.hint: A shady damp corner where leaves are left to pile up and rot. The messy bit is the point here, not the tidy bit.

wolverine.diet: Marmots, hares, and ptarmigan when it can catch them; frozen dead animals when it cannot; berries in late summer
wolverine.shelter: Tunnels dug metres down into deep spring snow, usually beside a fallen boulder or log, with food stored in side rooms
wolverine.preferredHabitat: Big, empty, high country with broken rock, and snow that lasts into late spring
wolverine.fact: A wolverine can smell a dead animal buried under three metres of snow, dig it out, and then drive a bear off it. It does all that in a body about the size of a small dog.
wolverine.role: The biggest weasel in the world, and the mountain's great scavenger. It is now the top hunter on these peaks. It roams huge distances. It kills marmots, hares, and ptarmigan when it gets the chance, and lives off frozen dead animals when it does not. Its jaws are built to crack frozen bone. Snow is its fridge. It stores food in drifts and dens deep inside them. So a female can only raise young where the snow holds into late spring. That makes it the first animal to go when winters get short. And nothing up here will argue with it over a dead animal.
wolverine.hint: What is needed here is space and snow, not views. Drifts deep enough to last into late spring, for the den and the food store. Broken rock to travel through. And marmots and hares already on the mountain. This is the last hunter to arrive.

bottlenose-dolphin.diet: Fish that swim in schools, above all anchovy, plus squid and fish from the bottom
bottlenose-dolphin.shelter: Builds none. It travels and sleeps at sea in a small group, with half its brain awake at a time
bottlenose-dolphin.preferredHabitat: Water close in along an open beach, with strong surf and fish schools offshore
bottlenose-dolphin.fact: Every dolphin makes up its own whistle. The others copy that whistle back when they want to call it over. Along an open beach, these dolphins hunt right inside the breaking waves they are herding fish against.
bottlenose-dolphin.role: Fast, sociable hunters that work the surf in small groups. They push anchovy schools up against the breaking waves until the fish have nowhere left to go. They are quick and clever enough to catch almost anything that schools here. And they are still not the biggest thing in the water.
bottlenose-dolphin.hint: Deep water to travel through, cold currents and kelp edges to hold the fish, and real breaking surf, because that is where the hunting happens.

orca.diet: Sea mammals: harbor seals most of all, plus dolphins, sea lions, and gray whale calves
orca.shelter: None on land. It rests at the surface in deep water with its family
orca.preferredHabitat: Cold deep water close to shore, where the sea floor drops away by the kelp edge, within reach of seal resting rocks
orca.fact: Orcas live in families that never split up, and different families eat completely different food. The ones that hunt this coast eat only mammals. They go silent to do it, with no clicks and no calls, because a seal can hear a talking orca coming from a long way off.
orca.role: The top of this coast, with nothing above it. A family of mammal-hunting orcas patrols the edge where the sea floor drops away. They listen at seal rocks. In spring they shadow gray whales passing through with calves. When they come into a bay, every seal on the rocks goes still and silent.
orca.hint: The last and hardest animal to bring back. Deep water pressed right up against the shore, and something big to hunt. Bring the seals back first, because the seals are the whole draw.

desert-millipede.diet: Dead leaves, stems, seed husks, and other dry plant litter on the ground
desert-millipede.shelter: Buried in soil and tucked under leaves and flat rocks by day; out walking on damp nights
desert-millipede.preferredHabitat: Drifts of dead leaves under shrubs, with flat rocks and soft soil nearby
desert-millipede.fact: A desert millipede spends most of the year underground. Then it pours out by the hundreds after the first summer storm. Touch one and it coils into a tight spiral like a cinnamon bun. It also oozes a bitter brown liquid that stains your fingers for days.
desert-millipede.role: The litter shredder. It chews dead leaves, stems, and husks into crumbs. Termites and tiny soil life can then finish the job. That is how dead plants become soil again out here. It has hundreds of legs and no hurry at all. Armor and a foul chemical mean it can afford to stroll. Scorpions and roadrunners eat it anyway.
desert-millipede.hint: Let the leaves drift up under the shrubs, and leave a flat rock to crawl beneath. Damp leaves are both dinner and hiding place. Bare hot sand is neither.

harris-hawk.diet: Jackrabbits, ground squirrels, quail, woodrats, and lizards
harris-hawk.shelter: A big stick nest wedged in the arms of a tall cactus or a thorny tree, built and guarded by the whole family
harris-hawk.preferredHabitat: Open scrub with tall cactus and trees to nest in and watch from
harris-hawk.fact: These are the only birds of prey in the world that hunt in packs. A family of five or six spreads out. Some crash into a thorn bush to panic a rabbit while the others wait on the far side. And when there is nowhere good to perch, they stand on each other's backs, three birds high.
harris-hawk.role: The top hunter by day. It works the same desert the coyote works at night. Two or three generations live together all year. They share every kill, help feed each other's chicks, and take turns on lookout. That teamwork lets them bring down jackrabbits far heavier than one bird could handle alone. They need tall lookouts above open ground, and a big cactus strong enough to hold a family nest.
harris-hawk.hint: One bird is never the whole story. A family needs a tall cactus strong enough to hold the nest, high lookouts all around it, and open ground with rabbits crossing it.

bald-eagle.diet: Mostly fish, plus ducks, muskrats, and dead animals. Also anything it can bully out of another hunter's grip
bald-eagle.shelter: A huge stick nest in the top of the tallest living tree beside open water, added to every year
bald-eagle.preferredHabitat: Wide open water full of fish, with one very tall tree to watch it all from
bald-eagle.fact: A bald eagle would rather rob than fish. It follows otters and herons and pesters them until they drop their catch, then takes it. The nest it rebuilds every year can end up heavier than a small car.
bald-eagle.role: The top hunter of the marsh, and its biggest bully. It takes fish, ducks, and muskrats for itself. It kills herons at their nesting colonies. It spends much of the day stealing meals from otters and herons. So it can only settle somewhere those hunters are already doing well.
bald-eagle.hint: One huge old tree with a clear view over deep water. Enough fish to live on. And otters and herons below doing well enough to steal from.

luna-moth.diet: Hickory, walnut, sweetgum, and birch leaves as a caterpillar. The grown moth eats nothing at all
luna-moth.shelter: A papery cocoon spun inside a curled leaf. The leaf falls, and the cocoon lies buried in the dead leaves all winter
luna-moth.preferredHabitat: Old broadleaf woods with deep dead leaves left alone under the trees
luna-moth.fact: A grown luna moth has no mouth. It comes out with about a week to live. It never eats once, and it spends that whole week looking for a mate.
luna-moth.role: Luna moth caterpillars eat leaves and turn them into fat, high-energy insect bodies. Everything from bats to jays cashes that in. The long twisted tails on the back wings are an anti-bat trick. They spin as the moth flies and throw a bat's echo off target. So the bat grabs a tail streamer instead of the body. The cocoon spends winter in the fallen leaves. So a forest that gets raked loses its luna moths, even if every tree is still standing.
luna-moth.hint: Plant the leafy trees, then let the leaves lie where they fall. The cocoons spend the whole winter down in them.

blue-jay.diet: Acorns and beechnuts, caterpillars, beetles and other bugs, and eggs or chicks when it finds them
blue-jay.shelter: A cup of twigs and roots wedged in a fork high in a leafy tree, hidden by the leaves
blue-jay.preferredHabitat: Woods full of oaks, and their edges, with open ground nearby for burying acorns
blue-jay.fact: Blue jay feathers are not really blue. The color in them is brown. The blue is a trick of light bouncing off tiny air pockets. Crush one and the blue is gone.
blue-jay.role: One blue jay can carry five acorns at a time and bury a few thousand in one autumn. It picks the sound ones and pushes them into open ground. That makes jays the fastest tree planters in the forest, and the reason oaks spread uphill after a fire. Jays also copy hawk calls. Sometimes that clears a feeding spot. Sometimes it warns everything nearby that a real hawk has arrived. So the whole wood listens to them.
blue-jay.hint: Oaks, and a patch of soft open ground to bury the acorns in. Some get forgotten. Those are your next oak trees.

wood-frog.diet: Beetles, spiders, slugs, flies, and other small creatures from the forest floor
wood-frog.shelter: Shallow dead leaves and loose litter on the forest floor. It does not dig down below the frost
wood-frog.preferredHabitat: Damp broadleaf forest with fishless woodland pools that fill in spring and dry up by late summer
wood-frog.fact: A wood frog freezes solid every winter. Its heart stops. Two thirds of the water in its body turns to ice. In spring it thaws out and hops away.
wood-frog.role: Wood frogs are the first frog to call in spring. They breed in pools that dry up before fish can ever live in them. That is exactly why the tadpoles survive. Sugar floods their blood and stops their cells bursting while they are frozen. So they can sleep the winter under a few centimetres of leaves. Grown frogs eat their way through the small creatures in the dead leaves. Snakes and raccoons then eat them, which carries food up the chain.
wood-frog.hint: A pool that dries up in summer is the good kind. No fish means the tadpoles live. Keep deep leaves nearby to freeze in.

goshawk.diet: Squirrels, jays, grouse, rabbits, and woodpeckers, chased down inside the trees
goshawk.shelter: A wide stick nest against the trunk on a heavy branch, halfway up a big old tree
goshawk.preferredHabitat: Old forest with a high closed roof of leaves and open flying room under it
goshawk.fact: A goshawk hunts by crashing straight through the branches at full speed with its wings half folded. It will dive at anything that walks too near its nest, people included.
goshawk.role: The forest's top hunter by day, and the reason squirrels freeze against tree trunks. Short wide wings and a long steering tail let it turn inside a wood at speed. So it hunts under the leaves, not above them like a soaring hawk. It needs old forest with big branches to nest on, and clear space below to fly. That is why its arrival means the trees have finally grown up.
goshawk.hint: Grow the forest tall and leave the space below it open. A big branch to nest on, and room to fly hard under the leaves.

moose.diet: Pondweed and water lilies in summer, willow and aspen twigs in winter
moose.shelter: Beds pressed into willow thickets and shady marsh edge. In summer it stands chest-deep in water to get away from flies
moose.preferredHabitat: Marsh and pond edge with thick willow and clear shallow water full of underwater plants
moose.fact: A moose can hold its breath for a minute and walk along the bottom of a pond with its whole head under water, pulling plants up by the roots.
moose.role: Moose come to the wetland for salt. The underwater plants have it and forest leaves do not. A big one can pull 20 kilograms of pondweed a day out of the shallows. All that heavy feeding keeps open lanes through the plant beds, where ducks feed and fish shelter. The willow it eats in winter grows back thicker and lower, which is better cover for everything small. Its trails through the marsh turn into channels that hold water in dry summers.
moose.hint: Grow the underwater plant beds first, and keep the water clear enough for them. The draw here is what grows under the surface, not on the bank.

river-cooter.diet: Pondweed, algae, water lily leaves, and fallen fruit. Babies eat bugs first, then switch to plants
river-cooter.shelter: Sleeps wedged under sunken logs and root tangles. Spends the winter buried in the mud at the bottom
river-cooter.preferredHabitat: Slow, plant-filled water with logs to bask on and an open sunny bank to lay eggs in
river-cooter.fact: Whether the eggs hatch into males or females depends on how warm the nest is, not on the eggs. A cool nest makes brothers. A warm one makes sisters.
river-cooter.role: This is the wetland's big plant-eating turtle. It crops the underwater meadows so they do not choke the shallows. It also drops the seeds somewhere else, still whole. It has to bask for hours to get warm enough to digest all that plant food. That is why a log stacked with turtles is a sign of a working marsh. Its eggs and babies feed almost everything else, so it lays a lot of them.
river-cooter.hint: Logs in the sun to bask on, and a bare warm bank to bury eggs in. No warm spot means no way to digest dinner.

javelina.diet: Prickly pear pads, mesquite pods, agave hearts, roots, and tubers
javelina.shelter: The herd beds down in the shade of thick thorny scrub or under a rock ledge through the heat of the day
javelina.preferredHabitat: Desert scrub and dry washes with thick thorny cover and prickly pear
javelina.fact: A javelina eats prickly pear whole, spines and all. It also has a scent gland on its back so strong that a herd can find each other in the dark by smell alone.
javelina.role: Javelinas are the desert's cactus crushers. They crunch through pads that nothing else will touch, which stops prickly pear taking over a wash. They spread its seeds in their droppings too. Rooting for tubers turns over hard crusted soil and buries dead leaves, so seeds have somewhere to sprout after rain. They travel in herds of six to a dozen. The herd smell is also the alarm system, because their eyesight is terrible.
javelina.hint: Grow the prickly pear and leave a shady thorny tangle to bed down in. The herd sleeps out the middle of the day and feeds at dusk.

black-swift.diet: Flying ants, aphids, beetles, and mayflies caught in the air, often hundreds of metres up
black-swift.shelter: A cup of moss glued to a wet crack in the rock, behind or beside falling water. It can only be reached from the air
black-swift.preferredHabitat: Cliffs with cold running water and wide open sky above the treeline
black-swift.fact: A black swift can stay in the air for six months without landing once. It eats, drinks, and sleeps flying. The chick is left alone all day while its parents hunt bugs 50 km away.
black-swift.role: Swifts hoover up the swarms of bugs that rising air lifts onto the mountain. They carry that food back as one squashed pellet. One delivery a day is enough for a chick, because the load is packed so tight. The nest has to stay wet and out of reach. So these birds only turn up where a cliff crack has water running over it. They are among the very last summer visitors to arrive, and the first to leave for the Amazon.
black-swift.hint: Find the wettest, darkest crack in the cliff and keep the water running down it. Nothing will nest here if it can be walked to.

peregrine-falcon.diet: Other birds, caught in mid-air: ptarmigan, rosy-finches, swifts, pipits, and small ducks
peregrine-falcon.shelter: A bare dip kicked into gravel on a high cliff ledge. It builds no nest at all
peregrine-falcon.preferredHabitat: Steep cliffs and rock faces above open ground, with plenty of birds flying below
peregrine-falcon.fact: A diving peregrine hits about 380 km/h. That makes it the fastest animal alive. It has bony cones in its nostrils that slow the air down, so the dive does not burst its lungs.
peregrine-falcon.role: The mountain's hunter of the air. It takes almost all of its food in flight, striking from above with a closed fist instead of grabbing. It hunts birds and nothing else. So it is a direct check on the flocks of finches, pipits, and ptarmigan feeding across the slopes. It needs a quiet cliff ledge and clear air below. It needs nothing at all to build with, just loose gravel to scrape a hollow in.
peregrine-falcon.hint: A high ledge with loose gravel on it, and open sky underneath. Do not build a nest. All it takes is a dip kicked in the grit.

owl-limpet.diet: Algae, plankton, and scraps of food picked out of the sand, grain by grain
owl-limpet.shelter: Half buried on edge in rippled sand, in beds of hundreds at a time
owl-limpet.preferredHabitat: Sheltered sandy bottoms just below the low tide line, where the current is gentle
owl-limpet.fact: A living sand dollar is not white and smooth. It is purple, and covered in tiny moving spines. It uses them to walk and to pass food along to its mouth. The white disc with the flower pattern is the skeleton, after everything else has washed away.
owl-limpet.role: A whole bed of them stands half buried on edge, like coins in a slot. They all lean into the current to catch what drifts past. Where the water is rougher, they lie flat instead, so they do not get rolled away.
owl-limpet.hint: Clean rippled sand just below the tide line, somewhere sheltered enough that the current stays gentle.

octopus.diet: Shore crabs, clams, mussels, snails, and shrimp, cracked open or drilled through
octopus.shelter: A crack or an empty shell, with a rock pulled across behind it and a heap of empty shells outside the door
octopus.preferredHabitat: Rocky sea floor and deep tidepools with lots of cracks and cold, clean water
octopus.fact: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood, and it tastes everything it touches with its arms. The only hard part of it is its beak. So one the size of a dinner plate can squeeze through a hole the size of a grape.
octopus.role: The top hunter without a backbone on the rocky shore. The pile of empty crab and clam shells outside its den is the easiest way to find one. It can change color and skin texture in under a second to vanish against rock or kelp, even though it is colorblind. If a clam will not open, it drills a neat hole and puts in a drug that makes the shell relax. Each octopus works through a huge number of crabs, which keeps the grazers and cleaners of the tidepools in check.
octopus.hint: Broken rock with gaps to hide in, and plenty of crabs. Leave the shell pile outside the den alone. That pile is how you know somebody is home.

grasshopper-mouse.diet: Scorpions, centipedes, beetles, and other mice
grasshopper-mouse.shelter: Takes over a burrow another animal dug, then defends it
grasshopper-mouse.preferredHabitat: Open sandy flats with scattered brush and plenty of prey underfoot
grasshopper-mouse.fact: This mouse hunts scorpions, gets stung in the face, and carries on eating. Its body switches the venom's pain signal off. Then it stands up on its back legs and howls at the moon like a tiny wolf.
grasshopper-mouse.role: A mouse that decided to be a hunter. It keeps scorpions and big bugs in check. It is one of the only animals that can eat the most venomous creatures in the desert without flinching.
grasshopper-mouse.hint: An old burrow it can take over, and open ground to hunt across. It gets all its water from what it catches.

snow-bunting.diet: Seeds blown onto the snow, plus bugs in the short summer
snow-bunting.shelter: Deep in a crack in the rock, lined with feathers and fur against the cold
snow-bunting.preferredHabitat: Windswept ridges and stony ground where the snow blows clear
snow-bunting.fact: Snow buntings nest further north than any other songbird on Earth. They tuck so deep into rock cracks that the male has to feed the female in the dark while she sits on the eggs.
snow-bunting.role: A small bird that treats a blizzard as ordinary weather. Flocks drift across bare ridges, picking up seed the wind has stranded on the snow. They turn from white to warm brown as the season turns.
snow-bunting.hint: A deep, dry crack in the rock out of the wind, and open stony ground nearby where the snow blows clear.

groundhog.diet: Grass, clover, dandelions, and just about any soft green thing it can reach
groundhog.shelter: A burrow with several doors, a sleeping room lined with grass, and a separate toilet room
groundhog.preferredHabitat: Meadow edges with deep, well-drained soil it can dig through
groundhog.fact: A groundhog digs a burrow with a front door, a back door, a bedroom, and a separate room for the toilet. It moves about a tonne of soil doing it. In winter its heart slows to about five beats a minute.
groundhog.role: The meadow's earthmover. Its old burrows become homes for foxes, snakes, rabbits, and half the small animals here. So one groundhog's digging lasts for years after the digger has gone.
groundhog.hint: Deep, well-drained soil at the edge of the grass, with a bolt-hole close by. It wants a place to dig more than a place to hide.

opossum.diet: Almost anything: bugs, fruit, eggs, dead animals, and a huge number of ticks
opossum.shelter: Sleeps the day in a hollow log or a borrowed burrow. It rarely uses the same one twice
opossum.preferredHabitat: Brushy edges with hollow wood, water nearby, and plenty to scavenge
opossum.fact: When an opossum plays dead, it is not acting. It faints. The body goes stiff, the tongue lolls out, and it gives off a smell like something long dead. It cannot snap out of it for several minutes, even if you walk away.
opossum.role: The meadow's clean-up crew. It eats what everything else has left, including dead animals and huge numbers of ticks. It is the only animal here that carries its young around on its back.
opossum.hint: Hollow wood to sleep the day away in, and berries within a night's walk. It moves house all the time, so give it more than one option.
